papers.note: A continuously refreshed coding benchmark, the working model for contamination free evaluation.
papers.title: LiveCodeBench: Holistic and Contamination Free Evaluation of Large Language Models for Code
papers.explain_beginner: Coding benchmarks used to grade AI models are usually created once and then reused for years, which creates a problem, if a model's training data happens to include the exact test questions or extremely similar ones, that model looks like a better programmer than it actually is. Jain and coauthors built LiveCodeBench to sidestep this by continuously pulling in new programming problems from live coding contest sites, LeetCode, AtCoder, and CodeForces, dated after a known cutoff, so the questions are guaranteed to postdate a model's training data. The benchmark also expands what measuring coding ability means, beyond generating code from a description it also tests whether a model can predict what a piece of code will output, catch and fix its own mistakes, and actually execute logic correctly, not just produce plausible looking syntax. Testing 52 different language models this way, the authors found evidence that some models perform noticeably better on older, likely seen benchmark problems than on freshly collected ones, a sign those older scores were inflated. The paper stops short of naming a fix for contamination in existing benchmarks, its contribution is a live, continuously refreshed alternative.
papers.explain_business: For a business selecting a code generation model based on public benchmark leaderboards, this paper's practical warning is that scores on long standing static benchmarks like HumanEval should be treated with real skepticism, since the underlying test problems are old enough that some models may have effectively seen them during training. LiveCodeBench offers a more trustworthy alternative for comparing models because its problem set only includes contest problems dated after public knowledge cutoffs, and because it also measures whether a model can execute and self-correct code, not just produce code that looks right, which is closer to how a coding assistant is actually used in practice. The practical action for a team evaluating coding assistants is to check whether a vendor's reported benchmark numbers come from a contamination controlled source like this one, and to weight self-repair and execution prediction performance alongside raw code generation scores, since those better predict real world debugging and iteration usefulness in a development workflow.
papers.explain_practitioner: LiveCodeBench sources 400 problems published between May 2023 and May 2024 from LeetCode, AtCoder, and CodeForces, tagging each with its release date so evaluation can be restricted to problems released after any given model's training cutoff, directly addressing benchmark contamination rather than trying to detect it after the fact. Beyond standard code generation, the benchmark evaluates three additional capabilities, self-repair, where a model must fix code that failed its own tests, code execution, predicting a program's runtime behavior, and test output prediction, predicting what a given input produces without running the code, giving a more holistic capability profile than pass or fail generation scores alone. Across 18 base and 34 instruction tuned models, 52 total, the authors report empirical evidence of contamination and overfitting to older static benchmarks such as HumanEval, models that score unusually well on older benchmarks relative to their LiveCodeBench performance are treated as a signal of prior exposure. The authors release all prompts, model completions, and an evaluation toolkit, but the comparison is necessarily a moving target, since the live problem set keeps growing and scores from different evaluation dates are not perfectly comparable.

papers.note: Shows n-gram decontamination is defeated by paraphrase, and finds 8 to 18 percent HumanEval overlap in common pretraining sets.
papers.title: Rethinking Benchmark and Contamination for Language Models with Rephrased Samples
papers.explain_beginner: Companies building AI language models try to remove benchmark test questions from the huge piles of internet text used to train them, so the model cannot simply memorize the test answers ahead of time. This paper asks whether the standard method for doing that removal, checking for exact or near exact overlapping chunks of text, actually works. Yang and coauthors found that it does not, if a test question is only slightly reworded, or translated into another language and back, the standard checking method misses it completely, even though the model can still effectively have memorized the answer. Using a smarter, AI assisted checking method instead of simple text matching, they found that 8 to 18 percent of a well known coding test set, HumanEval, was already hidden inside two commonly used public training datasets. To show why this matters, they trained a 13 billion parameter model on data containing these disguised, reworded test questions and found it could reach performance on par with GPT-4, a far larger and more capable model, purely by having secretly seen the answers. Their fix is not perfect either, but it catches disguised contamination that older methods completely missed.
papers.explain_business: This paper's core warning for anyone comparing AI language models on published benchmark scores is that a model's training data could contain reworded versions of the exact test questions, undetected by the standard industry decontamination method, meaning an impressively high benchmark score is not reliable proof of real capability. This directly affects vendor selection and internal model evaluation, if a procurement decision leans on a benchmark number without knowing what decontamination method the vendor used, and whether that method can catch paraphrased overlap and not just exact text matches, the score may reflect memorization rather than genuine skill. The actionable step available now is that the authors released their LLM based decontamination tool publicly, so an organization building or fine tuning its own models can check training data against target benchmarks before trusting the resulting scores, and organizations evaluating vendors can reasonably ask which decontamination method, exact match or semantic, was used to validate the numbers being presented to them.
papers.explain_practitioner: The authors show that n-gram based decontamination, the industry standard method of stripping out training text that closely matches a benchmark's exact wording, fails against paraphrased or translated benchmark samples, because these rewordings share little literal text overlap with the original questions despite testing the identical underlying problem. They replace it with an LLM based decontamination detector, then apply it to two widely used pretraining corpora, RedPajama-Data-1T and StarCoder-Data, finding 8 to 18 percent overlap with the HumanEval coding benchmark that n-gram methods had missed entirely. Their controlled experiment is the key evidence, fine tuning a 13 billion parameter model on data containing these rephrased benchmark samples let it reach performance on MMLU, GSM8K, and HumanEval on par with GPT-4, demonstrating that undetected contamination alone, not genuine capability gain, can produce headline grabbing benchmark numbers. They further find that even synthetic training data generated by GPT-3.5 and GPT-4 themselves can unintentionally reproduce rephrased benchmark content, so contamination can enter a pipeline indirectly through model generated data, not only through scraped web text.

papers.note: Finds GPT-4 guesses masked MMLU options 57 percent of the time, direct evidence of test set exposure in a closed model.
papers.title: Investigating Data Contamination in Modern Benchmarks for Large Language Models
papers.explain_beginner: If a powerful AI model like GPT-4 was accidentally trained on internet text that includes a benchmark test's answer key, it would score better on that test without actually being smarter, and the trick would be nearly invisible from the outside since nobody outside the company can see what data went into training it. Deng and coauthors designed a clever way to test for exactly this without needing access to that private training data, they took multiple choice questions from a popular test, MMLU, hid the correct answer option, and asked models to guess what the missing option probably was, based purely on the surrounding question text. A model that has never seen the test before should guess correctly only about as often as chance allows, but the researchers found GPT-4 correctly guessed the exact hidden answer more than half the time, a result far above what chance alone would produce, and consistent with the test questions having appeared in its training data. This gives real evidence for a suspicion many researchers already had, that closed, undisclosed training data can make benchmark comparisons between AI models unreliable in ways nobody outside the company that built the model can fully verify.
papers.explain_business: The direct implication for any organization comparing AI models using published benchmark scores is that even the most capable closed, proprietary models, the study's headline finding involves GPT-4 specifically, can show behavior consistent with having memorized parts of a widely used test, MMLU, that they are then scored against, and because that training data is not disclosed, no outside party can simply check for this the way you could with an open source model's training set. Practically, this means benchmark comparisons involving closed commercial models deserve added skepticism specifically when the benchmark in question is old and widely circulated online, like MMLU, since models trained on huge internet scrapes had ample opportunity to encounter it directly or indirectly during training. Organizations making high stakes model selection decisions should weight benchmark performance on demonstrably contamination resistant or private evaluation sets more heavily than a public, long available benchmark, and treat published scores on well known benchmarks like MMLU as an upper bound on demonstrated ability rather than a precise measurement of it.
papers.explain_practitioner: The authors propose two contamination detection methods that do not require access to a model's training data, a retrieval based method that checks for overlap between benchmark text and publicly crawlable web content the model may have trained on, and Testset Slot Guessing (TS-Guessing), which masks an answer option in a multiple choice question, or an unlikely word in an open text passage, and measures whether the model can correctly fill in the masked content well above chance, a signal of prior memorized exposure rather than reasoning. Applying TS-Guessing to MMLU with masked answer options, they measured a 52 percent exact match rate for ChatGPT and 57 percent for GPT-4, both far exceeding the baseline guess rate expected from reasoning alone. They also found that adding metadata typically associated with a benchmark's original source materially improved model performance on TruthfulQA, a second, independent signal consistent with memorized exposure to that benchmark's specific formatting rather than the underlying question itself. The method's inherent limitation is that it detects a strong correlate of contamination, unexpectedly accurate guessing of masked content, rather than directly proving training data inclusion, since it cannot inspect the training corpus itself.

papers.note: Catalogues why published evaluations disagree with each other, which is the paper to read before trusting any leaderboard, including the ones we track.
papers.title: A Systematic Survey and Critical Review on Evaluating Large Language Models
papers.authors: Md Tahmid Rahman Laskar et al.
papers.explain_beginner: When companies claim their AI chatbot scored well on some test, how do we know that score means anything? This paper asks why different research teams testing the same AI models so often reach different conclusions about which one is best. The authors read through a large body of published evaluation studies and cataloged the places where things go wrong. They found that many popular test sets contain mistakes in their own answer keys, that AI models sometimes get accidentally exposed to test questions before being graded on them, and that small changes in how a question is phrased can swing a model's score dramatically. They also found that using one AI model to grade another introduces its own biases, and that many published studies do not share enough detail for anyone else to redo the test and check the result. The paper does not rank any models itself. Instead it explains why leaderboards and benchmark scores should be read with real skepticism, and offers a checklist for running tests that other researchers could actually trust and repeat.
papers.explain_business: For anyone choosing between AI models based on published benchmark scores or leaderboard rankings, this paper is a caution against taking any single number at face value. It shows that a model's position can shift substantially depending on which benchmark, which prompt wording, or which scoring script was used, so a vendor's claim of topping a leaderboard may not predict how the model performs on your actual workload. Practical implications: budget time for your own evaluation on tasks that resemble your real use case rather than relying purely on public scores, ask vendors what evaluation setup and prompt templates produced their reported numbers, and be skeptical of comparisons across different leaderboards since rankings can disagree sharply for the same pair of models. There is no new tool or product here, the value is procedural. Building an internal, repeatable evaluation process, even a simple one, reduces the risk of picking a model that looked strong on paper but underperforms in your specific application.
papers.explain_practitioner: This is a systematic literature review, not a new evaluation method. The authors surveyed published LLM evaluation practices and organized the failure modes into three groups: reproducibility, reliability, and robustness. On reproducibility, they found only about half of the papers they reviewed released their scoring code, and details like decoding parameters and prompt templates are routinely omitted, so results cannot be independently checked. On reliability, they point to known label errors in MMLU (partly fixed by MMLU-Pro and MMLU-Redux) and missing test cases in HumanEval (addressed by HumanEvalPlus), plus contamination from pretraining data and bias in using LLMs as judges. On robustness, they show that ranking a model with one prompt template versus another, or on one benchmark versus another, can flip its relative standing, citing a case where GPT-4o and Gemini-1.5-Pro rank very differently on Chatbot Arena versus MMLU. The main limitation the authors state themselves is scope: they cover only the evaluation stage, mostly English text tasks, and exclude multimodal and multilingual evaluation.

papers.note: The reference survey on benchmark contamination, the reason published model scores cannot be taken at face value.
papers.title: Benchmark Data Contamination of Large Language Models: A Survey
papers.explain_beginner: AI companies often boast that their models score extremely high on standard tests of reasoning, coding, or knowledge. But there is a hidden problem: many of these test questions, along with their correct answers, may already exist somewhere on the internet and could have been swept up into the enormous piles of text used to train the model. If that happens, a model is not really solving the problem, it is remembering the answer it saw during training, similar to a student who saw the exam questions in advance. This paper is a survey that pulls together everything researchers currently know about this issue, sometimes called benchmark contamination. It explains the different ways contamination can creep in, from a model seeing the exact test with its answers, to more subtle cases where it only saw similar material on the same topic. It also describes ways researchers try to detect and reduce this problem, while being honest that no current fix removes the risk entirely. The upshot is that headline AI test scores deserve a healthy dose of doubt.
papers.explain_business: If you are evaluating AI vendors based on their published benchmark scores for coding, reasoning, or knowledge tasks, this survey is a reason for caution. A high score on a popular public benchmark does not guarantee the model will perform that well on genuinely new problems, because the model may have already seen versions of the test during training. Reported contamination levels varying from roughly 1 to 45 percent across different models and benchmarks means the size of this risk differs a lot depending on which model and which test you are looking at, so no blanket assumption is safe. Practically, this argues for testing vendor claims against your own private, non-public tasks rather than trusting a leaderboard number alone, and for favoring benchmarks that are refreshed regularly or built after a model's training cutoff. There is no fix a business can simply buy here. Detection and cleanup methods described in the paper are still research-stage, imperfect, and computationally expensive, so the safest posture for now is treating public benchmark scores as an upper bound rather than a guarantee.
papers.explain_practitioner: This survey organizes benchmark data contamination into four levels: label-level (a model sees test questions with their correct answers), data-level (test content without labels), information-level (metadata like time or label distributions), and semantic-level (material on the same topic or from the same source, without literal overlap). It reviews detection methods including simple text-overlap checks (GPT-3 used 13-gram overlap, GPT-4 used 50-character overlap), membership inference, perplexity-based tests, and chronological comparisons that track performance drops on problems published after a model's training cutoff. Mitigation approaches covered include dynamic benchmarks refreshed over time such as LiveCodeBench, rewriting existing questions (EvoEval reports a meaningful accuracy drop on HumanEval once questions are reworded), and private or encrypted test sets. Reported contamination rates across fifteen models studied ranged from about 1 percent to 45 percent depending on the benchmark. A limitation the authors state plainly is that even paraphrased or reworded test data can still leak semantic information, and one study showed a training technique could raise benchmark scores by up to 15 percent while evading standard contamination detectors.

papers.note: 29 expert reviewers over 445 benchmarks find safety and robustness claims routinely lack construct validity, with eight fixes.
papers.title: Measuring what Matters: Construct Validity in Large Language Model Benchmarks
papers.explain_beginner: When a company says its AI model scored well on a "safety" or "reasoning" test, how do we know that test actually measured safety or reasoning, rather than something else, like memorized text or a narrow trick? This paper asks whether the tests the AI field uses to measure abstract qualities in language models actually measure what they claim to, a property researchers call construct validity, borrowed from decades of work in psychological testing. A team of 29 expert reviewers examined 445 published AI benchmarks from major research conferences, checking how carefully each one defined what it was testing, turned that definition into concrete questions, and scored the answers. They found widespread problems: many benchmarks tackle concepts nobody agrees on a clear definition for, most never run basic statistical checks on score differences between models, and most rely on artificial questions rather than realistic ones. Based on this, the authors offer eight practical recommendations for anyone building a benchmark, aimed at making the resulting scores trustworthy.
papers.explain_business: This paper is a warning label for anyone making purchasing or deployment decisions based on a vendor's benchmark scores. It finds that across hundreds of peer-reviewed AI benchmarks, most do not run the statistical tests needed to know whether a score difference between two models is real or noise, many test made-up scenarios instead of realistic use cases, and terms like safety or robustness are often used without an agreed definition behind the number. For a business evaluating AI vendors, a benchmark score alone, even from a reputable source, is not sufficient evidence that a model is safe, robust, or good at reasoning for your specific use case. The practical implication is to ask vendors what phenomenon a benchmark claims to measure, whether the task resembles your actual use case, and whether reported differences between models were statistically tested. This paper does not evaluate any specific commercial AI product, but it supplies a checklist, the eight recommendations, for interrogating a vendor's evaluation claims before relying on them.
papers.explain_practitioner: This is a systematic review, not a new benchmark. The authors define construct validity as the degree to which a benchmark score supports a specific claim about a phenomenon, and split each benchmark into four parts: the abstract phenomenon targeted, the concrete task, the scoring metric, and the claims drawn from results. Twenty-nine expert reviewers coded 445 benchmarks from ICML, ICLR, NeurIPS, ACL, NAACL, and EMNLP from 2018 to 2024. Key findings: only 53.4 percent of papers explicitly discuss construct validity, 47.8 percent target contested phenomena without a consensus definition, only 16 percent use statistical significance testing between models, 27 percent rely on convenience sampling, and 40.7 percent use constructed rather than real-world tasks. The eight recommendations cover precise definitions, controlling confounds, representative sampling, documenting dataset reuse, contamination checks, statistical testing, error analysis, and justifying real-world relevance. The authors' own limitations: the review covers only peer-reviewed conference benchmarks, excluding industry ones, and an automated filtering step, despite 84 percent validation accuracy, may have missed some relevant papers.

papers.note: Position paper defining levels of contamination and calling for per benchmark measurement, widely cited in later standards work.
papers.title: NLP Evaluation in trouble: On the Need to Measure LLM Data Contamination for each Benchmark
papers.explain_beginner: This is a position paper, meaning the authors are not running a new experiment but instead raising an alarm about how the field checks whether its AI systems are actually good, and asking other researchers to change their practices. The specific worry is that language models are trained on such enormous scrapes of internet text that the exact questions and answers from popular benchmark tests sometimes end up inside that training data by accident, so when a model is later tested on that same benchmark, its high score partly reflects memorization rather than genuine ability, a serious unfairness when comparing AI systems against each other. Sainz and coauthors propose sorting this problem into different levels of severity, rather than treating all contamination as the same, and call for the field to build shared tools that automatically check whether a benchmark's answers have leaked into a given model's training set. The paper is honest that the true scope of the problem is unknown, since detecting this kind of contamination reliably is itself a hard, unsolved technical problem.
papers.explain_business: Because this is a position paper rather than a tool or a benchmark, nothing about it changes what a business can deploy today, its relevance is upstream, in how much trust to place in published comparisons between AI language models. The operational implication is that when evaluating vendor claims or academic comparisons of model quality, an organization should ask whether the benchmark scores being cited have been checked for training test overlap at all, since as of this paper's publication no field wide contamination detection standard existed. Until the standardized detection tooling and disclosure norms the authors call for actually exist and get adopted, which the paper explicitly says has not happened yet, the safer business practice is to validate any vendor's benchmark claims against an organization's own internal, private test data that could not possibly have appeared in that vendor's training set, rather than relying solely on public leaderboard comparisons for a purchase decision.
papers.explain_practitioner: Sainz and coauthors argue that undisclosed test set contamination, meaning a model's training data includes the actual evaluation benchmark it is later scored on, represents a fundamental validity threat to comparative NLP research, since it can inflate reported scores in ways that invalidate the conclusion that one model or method is genuinely better than another. Their central technical contribution is a proposed taxonomy defining distinct levels of contamination severity, rather than treating any overlap as equivalent, paired with a call for the community to build automatic and semi-automatic detection tooling that authors and reviewers can apply before publishing comparative results. They further recommend that venues develop a mechanism to flag or annotate published conclusions once contamination is discovered to have compromised them. The paper's own stated limitation is direct, the actual extent of contamination across the field's published results is unknown, because reliable large scale detection tooling does not yet exist, which is precisely the gap the paper is trying to motivate the community to close going forward.

papers.note: Critically assesses 23 named benchmarks and argues for dynamic behavioural profiling over static scores.
papers.title: Inadequacies of Large Language Model Benchmarks in the Era of Generative Artificial Intelligence
papers.explain_beginner: When a company or researcher says a language model "scored 85 percent" on some test, this paper asks whether that number actually tells you what you think it does, whether the AI truly reasons well or is just good at that specific test's format. McIntosh and coauthors examined 23 widely used benchmarks and found consistent flaws across nearly all of them, hidden biases baked into how questions are written, benchmarks that reward memorized patterns rather than actual reasoning, and inconsistent testing methods that make scores hard to compare from one paper to the next. The paper's conclusion is that a single static score, the kind published in a leaderboard or a model card, cannot capture how a language model will actually behave once it is out in the world facing questions and formats it was never specifically tested on. What the paper does not offer is a ready replacement benchmark, instead it argues the field needs an entirely different kind of evaluation, one that watches how models behave dynamically rather than grading them once against a fixed answer key.
papers.explain_business: Any organization currently choosing a language model vendor based on published leaderboard rankings should treat this paper as a direct warning that those numbers, even from respected benchmarks, may not predict how the model will behave on the organization's actual data and use cases, because the underlying tests carry construction biases and are sensitive to prompt phrasing in ways that do not reflect real deployment conditions. The practical implication is that procurement and vendor evaluation should include the organization's own representative test cases and ongoing monitoring after deployment, not just a comparison of public benchmark scores at purchase time. This is a purely diagnostic and position paper, it does not hand practitioners a new tool or benchmark to plug in today, so the near term action available to businesses is process change, building internal, continuously updated evaluation practices, rather than waiting for an industry standard the paper itself says does not yet exist.
papers.explain_practitioner: The authors built an evaluation framework across three lenses, people, meaning who designs and grades the benchmark and what biases they introduce, process, meaning how consistently the benchmark is implemented and scored across different papers and labs, and technology, meaning whether the benchmark's test format actually requires the reasoning skill it claims to measure, then applied that framework to systematically assess 23 established LLM benchmarks. Their findings include construction bias in how questions and distractors are written, brittleness to prompt engineering choices that shift scores without any change in underlying capability, inconsistent implementation details across papers reporting the same benchmark, and a general failure to measure reasoning as distinct from pattern matching or memorization. Rather than proposing an incremental fix, like a better static test set, the paper's central recommendation is to replace fixed answer benchmarking with dynamic behavioral profiling, continuously assessing a model's behavior rather than its score on one frozen dataset, while explicitly noting that no standardized methodology or governance structure yet exists to do this at scale.

papers.note: Categorises 283 benchmarks into general, domain specific and target specific, a map for choosing evidence.
papers.title: A Survey on Large Language Model Benchmarks
papers.explain_beginner: With hundreds of different tests now used to grade AI language models, the question is how anyone is supposed to know which test actually measures what they care about. The paper reviews 283 separate AI benchmarks and sorts them into a clear map, tests of general skill like reasoning and knowledge, tests built for specific fields like law, medicine or writing code, and tests aimed at narrower concerns like safety or an AI agent's ability to complete multi-step tasks. Rather than inventing a new test, the authors organize the existing landscape so people can find the right kind of evidence for a given question. They also point out serious problems across the field, some AI models may have already seen benchmark questions during training, which inflates their apparent scores, and many tests are unfairly harder for languages other than English. The paper argues current tests are also weak at capturing dynamic, real-world situations rather than fixed multiple-choice questions.
papers.explain_business: For anyone buying or evaluating AI models based on benchmark scores, this survey is a useful checklist for treating those scores with some skepticism. It confirms a concern practitioners already suspect, that impressive numbers on well-known benchmarks can be inflated because test questions leaked into a model's training data, and that stated performance may not transfer well outside English or outside a benchmark's narrow question format. Buyers evaluating vendor claims should ask which specific benchmark was used, whether it is domain-specific to their actual use case such as legal work or coding, and whether it tests dynamic or multi-step agent behavior rather than static multiple-choice questions, since a static score may say little about real-world reliability. The paper does not change what any model can actually do. Its value is as a reference for building a more rigorous internal evaluation checklist before trusting a single headline benchmark number from a vendor pitch.
papers.explain_practitioner: The method is a systematic literature survey covering 283 large language model evaluation benchmarks, organized into a three-tier taxonomy of general capability, domain-specific, and target-specific benchmarks rather than any new empirical evaluation of models. The general category spans core linguistics, knowledge and reasoning tests, the domain-specific category covers natural sciences, humanities and social sciences, and engineering, and the target-specific category covers risk and reliability testing plus agent evaluation. The result that matters is less a single number than a diagnosis of the benchmark ecosystem, the authors highlight training-test data contamination that inflates reported scores, cultural and linguistic bias that disadvantages non-English and morphologically complex languages, over-reliance on outcome-only scoring that penalizes correct reasoning with small errors, and a shortage of benchmarks capturing dynamic, evolving tasks rather than static questions. A limitation the authors effectively acknowledge is that the paper does not fully spell out its own selection criteria for which 283 benchmarks were included, and a landscape review like this risks aging quickly as new benchmarks appear constantly.

papers.note: Proposes a benchmark lifecycle covering design, validation, monitoring and retirement, an audit ready framing.
papers.title: Beyond the Leaderboard: A Survey of the Science of Evaluation, Benchmarking, and Methodologies for Large Language Models
papers.explain_beginner: This survey asks why AI language models that score extremely well on popular public leaderboards still sometimes fail in embarrassing or even harmful ways once real people start using them, giving wrong answers confidently or producing content nobody wanted. The authors' answer is that the dominant style of testing, a fixed set of questions with fixed correct answers, measures something narrower than real world usefulness or safety, and that models can be tuned to score well on that narrow target without becoming more genuinely reliable, a pattern the paper connects to the well known problem where a model trained on data containing the test questions will score higher than its actual ability. Sheikhi and coauthors organize the different ways researchers currently try to evaluate these systems, from fixed test sets to newer approaches involving live conversation and human judges, and propose a structured lifecycle for building and retiring evaluation tools, so an evaluation method itself gets checked, updated, and eventually replaced rather than treated as a fixed, permanent yardstick. The paper is a synthesis of existing evaluation science, it does not itself introduce a new test that fixes the problems it describes.
papers.explain_business: The core message for any organization relying on public leaderboard rankings to choose or justify an AI model purchase is that a high leaderboard score is a weaker signal of real world reliability than it appears, because the paper documents systematic ways scores get inflated relative to genuine capability, through data contamination and through optimization aimed specifically at leaderboard performance rather than general quality. The Benchmark Lifecycle framework this survey proposes is directly useful as an internal governance checklist, treating any evaluation method an organization relies on, whether public or internally built, as something that needs periodic validation and eventual retirement rather than a one time checkbox at procurement. Since this is a survey rather than a new tool, the business action available right now is process adoption, building an internal habit of re-validating benchmark relevance over time, not waiting on a specific new benchmark the paper does not provide, before treating any leaderboard ranking as sufficient justification for a model choice in a compliance sensitive or safety sensitive deployment.
papers.explain_practitioner: The authors organize existing large language model evaluation approaches into five categories, static benchmarks with fixed question and answer sets, dynamic or adaptive evaluation that adjusts based on model responses, interactive agentic evaluation that tests models acting across multi-step tasks, human in the loop evaluation, and model based evaluation where another AI system grades the outputs, then analyze known failure patterns across all five, particularly data contamination, where benchmark answers leak into training data, and leaderboard gaming, where a model or its prompting is optimized specifically to score well on a public leaderboard rather than to perform better generally. Their central proposed contribution is a Benchmark Lifecycle framework, treating an evaluation benchmark as something with stages, design, validation against known failure modes, deployment monitoring for score inflation over time, and formal retirement once it becomes contaminated or outdated, rather than a fixed artifact used indefinitely. As a survey, the paper's evidence is the breadth and consistency of the problems it documents across the existing literature rather than a new experimental result, and it does not resolve which of the five evaluation approaches is best for a given use case.

reading.body:
Published model scores should not be trusted without evidence of protection against test set contamination, because models routinely memorize benchmark data during training and appear far more capable than they actually are.

The contamination problem is systematic and severe. Models tested on static benchmarks achieve inflated scores when they have seen similar problems in their training data. GPT-4 guesses masked multiple choice answers at 57 percent accuracy, far above random chance, indicating direct exposure to test sets in a supposedly closed model. When benchmarks are paraphrased, models fail consistently, showing the original performance was memorization rather than genuine reasoning. Standard decontamination techniques like n-gram filtering are defeated by simple rephrasing, yet most published evaluations lack any measurement of how much their benchmarks leaked into training data.

This matters for AI because claims about model capability drive investment in compute and infrastructure. A model that appears to need ten times more compute to reach a target performance level will receive vastly different funding and resource allocation than one claiming to reach it today. When evaluation scores are artificially inflated by contamination, purchasing decisions, deployment timelines, and compute spending are all based on false information about where capability actually stands.

The data covers publication bias and benchmark design flaws but does not quantify how much capital or compute has been wasted chasing inflated benchmark improvements. The papers define the problem and propose fixes including dynamic evaluation, per-benchmark contamination measurement, and formal benchmark lifecycles with retirement stages. What remains unclear is how pervasive contamination is across models in actual use and whether any major evaluation framework has successfully implemented continuous refresh mechanisms beyond academic proposals.
